Read the architecture

Colors match the animations. Boxes nest inside their owning process; arrows carry calls or messages.

  • API processOS process

    Owns the HTTP server, app, event loop and tokenizer executor.

    SOURCEserve_api_server_and_model_worker() [SERVE:L60]
  • Uvicorn / ServerPython object

    Uvicorn's Server object handles HTTP and invokes the FastAPI ASGI app in the API process.

    SOURCEfastapi_config(app, server_settings=settings) [API:L482]
  • FastAPI appASGI application

    Routes and validates requests. Async request tasks share the API loop thread.

    SOURCEfastapi_app(settings, pipeline_settings) [API:L346]
  • uvloop event loopEvent-loop thread

    Runs ready callbacks and coroutines. The API and model worker each own a loop in their own process.

    SOURCEuvloop.run(serve()) [SERVE:L176] · ModelWorker.run() [WORKER:L338]
  • Tokenizer executorCPU thread pool

    CPU tokenization runs via run_in_executor(None, …) on executor threads in the API process.

    SOURCErun_with_default_executor() [TOKENIZER:L363]
  • ZeroMQ channelsIPC · Unix sockets

    Local ipc:// PUSH/PULL channels carry requests, responses and cancellation. Each drawn slot holds one request context; N is exact only in this teaching model.

    SOURCEgenerate_zmq_ipc_path() [IPC:L63] · ZmqConfig.__init__() [IPC:L250]
  • Model worker / schedulerSpawned OS process

    Owns pending work, batch selection and model execution. The scheduler runs on the worker's loop thread; it selects the next pass.

    SOURCEproc.start(ModelWorker(), alive, factory, config, ...) [WORKER:L801] · ModelWorker.run() [WORKER:L338]
  • CE / TG request setsCPU collections · worker

    CE holds prefill work; TG holds decoding contexts. These are worker-owned Python collections, not IPC channels or separate threads.

    SOURCETokenGenerationScheduler._retrieve_pending_requests() [TG_SCHED:L244] · TextBatchConstructor.construct_batch() [BATCH:L2254]
  • Batch constructorPython object · worker loop

    Chooses eligible work within batch, token and KV limits. It is called on the worker's loop thread. P = prefill; D = decode; work-tile counts are input tokens.

    SOURCETextBatchConstructor.construct_batch() [BATCH:L2254]
  • Model pipelinePython → compiled model

    Prepares inputs and calls the native runtime for selected model work. It returns per-request results; it is not another OS process.

    SOURCETextGenerationPipeline._execute() [TEXT:L594] · Execute, advance requests and release completed requests [TG_SCHED:L487]
  • KV managerHost bookkeeping + device pool

    Tracks request attention-cache ownership and reusable blocks. Releasing a finished request makes its blocks reusable while the backing pool remains allocated. This is resource management, not a mutex.

    SOURCEload_kv_manager() [KV_REGISTRY:L164] · TextBatchConstructor.release_request() [BATCH:L1066]
  • MAX runtime / user driverNative code · worker

    Submits compiled model work and manages device completion. Internal native threads sit behind this boundary.

    SOURCEPython session delegates to the native engine [ENGINE:L707]
  • OS GPU driverKernel boundary

    The operating system's device driver connects the user-space runtime to the GPU.

    BOUNDARY · reference atlas ↗
  • GPU deviceHardware

    Executes the selected model pass and holds device data, including model weights and KV cache.

    BOUNDARY · reference atlas ↗

What synchronizes the handoff?

◇ Admission gate

asyncio.Lock · coroutine mutual exclusion around the writable probe and send, inside the API process. It is released before awaiting model output; it is not another event loop.

SOURCEZmqModelWorkerProxy.__init__() [ZMQ:L56] · ZmqModelWorkerProxy.stream() [ZMQ:L105]
◎ Worker readiness

multiprocessing.Event · a process-shared readiness signal during startup. The API also awaits the channel connection.

SOURCEstart_model_worker() [WORKER:L759] · ZmqModelWorkerProxy.wait_until_connected() [ZMQ:L87]

Component colors identify owners; request colors indicate request state. SOURCE: pinned Python control flow. BOUNDARY: native runtime, OS and device. One ordinary, non-overlap worker per replica.

01

01 · Start inside the API process

One process. Different jobs.

Uvicorn speaks HTTP. FastAPI supplies MAX's routes and handlers. The uvloop event loop runs their ready async work on the same loop thread. CPU tokenization uses executor threads.

T1 marks that shared loop thread in every component. T2 / T3 mark example tokenizer executor threads. Only CPU jobs go to those threads; async request tasks resume on T1. R1 / R2 remain request IDs. Thread IDs and executor assignments are illustrative; real pool sizing and reuse vary.

The admission guard is an asyncio.Lock: coroutine mutual exclusion around probe → send. It is a synchronization primitive, not another event loop or a process-shared OS lock. An await can let a second task run even on one thread.

Try it Play with all roles present. Then choose No admission lock and compare R2. Remove the other roles to see why the API service needs them.

Two valid requests, a connected worker and one illustrative IPC slot. The worker initially stops pulling. Native/GPU execution is outside this view.

Tokenizer executor · API process

T2 / T3 · EXAMPLE LANESThese are teaching lanes: two jobs such as R1 and R2 can tokenize at once. MAX does not set the tokenizer pool to exactly two threads here.

SUBMIT · FROM T1T1 submits synchronous tokenization with run_in_executor(None, ...) and awaits it. None selects the event loop's default thread pool.

AWAIT · THE LOOP STAYS AVAILABLEThe request task pauses. A pool worker tokenizes while T1 runs other ready async tasks and handles I/O.

RETURN · RESUME ON T1When tokenization ends, its result resumes the waiting coroutine on T1. Requests can use any available worker.

POOL · REUSE AND REAL SIZINGWorkers are created as needed and reused; the maximum depends on Python and CPU count. Python 3.13: min(32, (process_cpu_count() or 1) + 4). With 8 CPUs, that is at most 12 workers.

THROUGHPUT · NOT A 2× PROMISETwo workers let separate jobs overlap, but do not guarantee twice the CPU throughput.

    02

    02 · Inside the model worker

    A batch, then another.

    The API has already admitted these requests. Inside the separate worker process, one loop calls the scheduler: pull → build → execute → advance / release → publish. No eligible work produces NO_PROGRESS, then an awaited backoff.

    CE is prompt processing (prefill); TG is continuation (decode). The constructor picks eligible work within batch, token and KV constraints. A running pass keeps its selected members. A partial prefill returns for another pass before it can produce its first token.

    The pipeline calls the native runtime and GPU. Request contexts stay in CPU memory; GPU tiles represent the selected work. Results are returned by request ID. Finished requests release block ownership; the backing KV pool remains allocated.

    Try it Compare GPU busy with KV pressure. Watch R2's waiting location, the unused batch slot, and the blocks becoming reusable. No requests shows the idle path.

    One ordinary non-overlap pipeline; small synthetic requests and an illustrative decode-first, chunked policy. The toy cache reserves prompt plus output blocks at entry. Actual allocation, preemption, overlap and priorities depend on configuration. This close-up begins after admission; cache waits are not HTTP 429.

Busy pass: its membership stays fixed; a later request waits for another pass.
Partial prefill: finish the whole prompt before emitting its first token.
KV pressure: already-admitted work waits; HTTP 429 is an API admission decision.
Release: request block ownership becomes reusable; the backing pool stays allocated.
One ordinary non-overlap pipeline; tiny queues, budgets and reservations are teaching choices.

        04 · Now the worker is busy

        There is room to wait.

        R1 is already generating. Send R2 while the worker is inside a model pass. Watch where R2 waits and when it joins a batch.

        With one batch slot, R2 waits for R1 to finish. With two slots and enough KV space, R2 can join a later pass while R1 is still decoding. A running pass keeps its selected members.

        Try it Send R2, then replay with two batch slots. Compare the waiting location.

          05

          05 · Keep sending work

          Watch backpressure reach the gate.

          Keep R1 decoding, then send a burst. The worker's pending-prefill queue M fills. It stops pulling from IPC. The request channel N then fills too.

          When the API proxy finds that connected channel unwritable, it raises RequestQueueFull. The HTTP handler returns 429 with Retry-After: 1 before streaming begins. Already admitted requests stay in the system.

          Try it Send a burst of six. Increase N and replay the same burst to see more waiting room.

          N = --max-queue-size
          M = --max-pending-requests
          Both default to unbounded in this pinned checkout. This scene sets finite example limits.

            06 · Look inside the loop

            A batch is one pass of work.

            R1 is decoding a response. R2 has a longer prompt. The scheduler builds each pass from eligible work, within batch, token and KV limits.

            This example gives decode one input token per request and uses the remaining budget for chunked prefill. A partial prompt returns for another pass. Completing prefill yields the first output token; ordinary decode then adds one token per selected request per pass.

            Try it Step through the five highlighted phases. Compare the pass history below the diagram.

              What these animations represent

              SOURCE Admission, the N/M backpressure chain, the worker loop and request cleanup follow this checkout's pinned source. BOUNDARY Device execution and OS lanes describe ownership; they are not GPU or Linux traces.

              The opening API-process lesson uses two valid requests and one connected IPC slot. Component removals and the alternative event loop are thought experiments. The no-lock trace selects a possible interleaving where two probes see room before either sends; it does not claim a captured race or queue overflow. Normal playback stops after the first output chunk.

              The second lesson starts inside the separate model worker after API admission. It uses the same teaching worker as the later stories to compare normal batches, a busy pass, KV pressure and an idle loop. CPU request markers, GPU work tiles, KV ownership blocks and response maps show distinct parts of the flow. The process diagrams do not imply a separate thread for each box.

              The diagrams use exact, small N-slot queues, artificial event durations, tiny token counts, one ordinary non-overlap worker and a simple chunked, decode-first policy. Real ZeroMQ high-water marks are approximate. MAX's batch strategy, token budgets, grammar readiness, adapters, cache availability and overlap settings can change the selected work and when results arrive.

              The toy worker conservatively reserves prompt plus output KV pages at batch entry. MAX allocates through its cache manager and can preempt/recompute or use configured transfer paths. A request waiting for cache space is already admitted; this simulation never converts that wait into an HTTP 429.

              M is checked against all_ce_reqs at the start of the iteration. The drawings keep unfinished prefill visible with waiting prefill. Decoders are separate. Both queue limits default to None (unbounded) in the pinned source; finite values here are teaching settings.

              The replica scene uses an external example router, one independent GPU allocation per replica and illustrative readiness delays. It does not model tensor parallelism or automatic scaling. Output buffering is grouped across response IPC, API and transport.

              Connect the moving requests to their lifecycle

              Three different kinds of state.

              The server can be ready while a request waits and an OS thread sleeps. Choose a path below, then step through its transitions. Each animation above also links its selected request back to this atlas.

              Server readiness and shutdown

              Teaching states for the complete serving instance. Each readiness gate belongs to a different owner.

              Request waiting, execution and streaming

              Teaching states group API and worker operations. Streaming can overlap later decode passes; cancellation is a cleanup request.

              One Linux thread: runnable, running, waiting

              A simplified OS-thread state machine. A suspended Python task and a sleeping OS thread belong to different layers.

              Selected state

              Runnable

              The OS thread can run and is waiting for CPU scheduling.

              Portable state machine and meaning
              Runnable -- CPU dispatch --> Running -- blocking wait --> Waiting
   ^                            |                          |
   +------ preempt / yield ------+                          |
   +---------------------- event / I/O wake ----------------+

Python task: await -> suspended -> resumed by its event loop
OS thread:  may keep running another callback; waits only when appropriate
GPU work:   queued -> executing -> completion; separate device dependencies
              Runnable

              Owner: Linux scheduler

              The OS thread can run and is waiting for CPU scheduling.

              NGINX: event-driven server architecture · libuv: design of the I/O event loop

              Running

              Owner: CPU thread

              The thread executes callbacks, Python code or native work on a CPU.

              uvloop.run(serve()) [SERVE:L176] · ModelWorker.run() [WORKER:L338]

              Waiting

              Owner: Kernel I/O / wait

              A thread is blocked on an event or I/O operation. Other threads can run.

              _read_ready() [PROC:L56] · ProcessManager.ready() [PROC:L201]

              Linux epoll: interest and ready lists · libuv: design of the I/O event loop

              CPU dispatch

              Runnable → Running

              Linux selects the runnable OS thread to execute.

              blocking wait

              Running → Waiting

              An idle event-loop thread can wait for I/O; an executor thread can wait for an Event.

              ProcessManager.ready() [PROC:L201]

              Linux epoll: interest and ready lists · libuv: design of the I/O event loop

              event / I/O arrives

              Waiting → Runnable

              The awaited event makes the thread eligible to execute again.

              Linux epoll: interest and ready lists · libuv: design of the I/O event loop

              preempt / yield CPU

              Running → Runnable

              Linux may schedule another runnable thread while this one retains its execution state.

              API process

              User space

              Owns the HTTP frontend, tokenizer and worker proxy.

              Interacts with

              Linux sockets, its event loop and the model worker through IPC.

              Back in the call stack

              cli_serve → serve_api_server_and_model_worker → lifespan

              • FastAPI is the ASGI application; Uvicorn is the HTTP server. Creating their Python objects prepares the frontend.
              • ServingTokenGeneratorSettings carries the model factory, configuration, tokenizer, task and memory plan. These are application inputs.
              • After worker readiness and IPC connectivity, TokenGeneratorPipeline connects HTTP handling to worker communication.

              Model-worker process

              User space

              Owns the initialized model pipeline, native session and request scheduler.

              Interacts with

              The API through IPC; files and RAM; the native device backend.

              Back in the call stack

              proc.start(ModelWorker()) → ModelWorker.run → model_factory

              • Python spawn starts a fresh interpreter with its own process address space and file-descriptor table.
              • The worker initializes the pipeline once and repeatedly calls scheduler.run_iteration(). It serves requests through this long-lived loop.
              • Its first alive.set() announces readiness after initialization; later signals can support heartbeat monitoring.

              Python multiprocessing: spawn and process lifecycle

              Linux processes and CPU threads

              Kernel

              Provide isolation and decide which runnable OS threads receive CPU time.

              Interacts with

              Both Python processes, executor threads and native-runtime threads.

              Back in the call stack

              multiprocessing.get_context("spawn"); executor and event-loop work

              • A PID identifies a process. Several OS threads can share that process's memory while having separate execution state.
              • Linux schedules CPU threads. MAX's model scheduler separately chooses requests for an inference pass.
              • A Python coroutine can suspend while its event-loop thread continues another callback. One process can contain threads in different states.

              proc.start(ModelWorker(), alive, factory, config, ...) [WORKER:L801] · ProcessManager.ready() [PROC:L201] · TextTokenizer._encode_text() [TOKENIZER:L769]

              uvloop / libuv event loop

              User space

              Runs ready callbacks and resumes Python tasks after awaited work becomes available.

              Interacts with

              Linux epoll, network/IPC readiness, timers and completed executor work.

              Back in the call stack

              uvloop.run(serve()); uvloop executes ModelWorker.run

              • uvloop implements Python's asyncio event-loop interface using libuv. The API and worker run separate loops in separate processes.
              • On Linux, libuv uses epoll for I/O readiness. Callbacks handle ready descriptors; idle connections retain state without continuous polling by Python.
              • CPU work that occupies an event-loop thread can delay other callbacks. The tokenizer and readiness wait use executor helpers in this source.

              uvloop.run(serve()) [SERVE:L176] · ModelWorker.run() [WORKER:L338] · TextTokenizer._encode_text() [TOKENIZER:L769] · ProcessManager.ready() [PROC:L201]

              Kernel

              libuv, TCP sockets and local Unix-domain sockets.

              TCP listener and connected sockets

              Kernel

              Maintain connection state and receive/send byte buffers.

              Interacts with

              The NIC/network stack and Uvicorn's event loop.

              NIC and Linux network driver

              Hardware + kernel

              Move network packets between the link and host buffers, then feed the TCP stack.

              Interacts with

              DMA-accessible host RAM, NAPI/interrupt processing and Linux sockets.

              Back in the call stack

              The network boundary behind server.serve and HTTP traffic

              • A typical receive path uses NIC descriptors and DMA into host buffers. Linux's network driver and NAPI process received work.
              • The TCP stack associates bytes with a connection, making its socket ready for user-space processing.
              • The API-to-worker ipc:// transport is local Unix IPC. Its messages take a local kernel path rather than travelling through the NIC.

              ZeroMQ and Unix-domain IPC

              User space + kernel

              Carry request contexts, responses and cancellation between the two processes.

              Interacts with

              API proxy PUSH/PULL endpoints and worker PUSH/PULL endpoints.

              Back in the call stack

              ZmqModelWorkerInterface → model_worker_queues / model_worker_proxy

              • Requests: API PUSH → worker PULL. Responses: worker PUSH → API PULL. Cancellation: API PUSH → worker PULL.
              • libzmq implements message framing and queues in user space. On Linux, its ipc:// transport uses Unix-domain sockets.
              • The API waits for request-channel connectivity during startup. Each process retains its own ordinary Python objects; IPC transfers encoded information.

              Readiness Event and process lifecycle

              User space + OS support

              Let the parent wait for a usable worker and notice worker exit or timeout.

              Interacts with

              Worker alive.set(), API executor wait and lifecycle FD monitoring.

              Back in the call stack

              await proc.ready(alive) → wait_until_connected()

              • The worker sets a multiprocessing Event after initialization. ProcessManager.ready() waits through run_in_executor and clears the Event after observing it.
              • The wait checks for timeout or an exited subprocess. First readiness and optional later heartbeat monitoring have different purposes.
              • Readiness is followed by the request-channel handshake. Only then does MAX return from lifespan startup and enter Uvicorn serving.

              Host virtual memory and RAM

              Kernel + hardware

              Back process heaps, native buffers, file pages and socket buffers.

              Interacts with

              API and worker address spaces, Linux memory mappings and device transfers.

              Back in the call stack

              TextGenerationPipeline.__init__; load_weights; device buffers

              • CPU pointers belong to a process virtual address space. Linux page tables map ordinary process pages to host RAM.
              • The API and worker have separate heaps. Sharing memory requires an explicit mechanism; an IPC message alone does not share an entire heap.
              • GPU VRAM and GPU device pointers belong to the device side. A driver-managed transfer or mapping connects the two domains when required.

              User space

              2. Report socket readiness to the event loop

              Owner

              Linux epoll → libuv / uvloop → Uvicorn

              Interaction

              epoll reports ready I/O. libuv dispatches the callback, and Uvicorn reads and interprets HTTP bytes for the FastAPI application.

              State change

              The application's request handling becomes runnable.

              3. Prepare a request context

              Owner

              API frontend and tokenizer

              Interaction

              4. Send the context on the request channel

              Owner

              API request PUSH → local Unix IPC

              Interaction

              ZeroMQ encodes and sends a message through ipc://. Linux supplies the local Unix-domain socket transport between the processes.

              State change

              Request data crosses the process boundary without making an HTTP or NIC hop.

              5. Select queued model work

              Owner

              Worker request PULL → MAX scheduler

              Interaction

              The worker receives contexts. MAX's scheduler chooses eligible work and calls the initialized pipeline; Linux schedules the CPU threads executing that code.

              State change

              Selected requests become an inference pass; other requests remain waiting.

              Owner

              Worker → native session → GPU driver / device

              Interaction

              pipeline.execute() uses loaded executable state and device buffers. The native backend submits required transfers and compute with device dependencies.

              State change

              The GPU has work to execute for the selected requests.

              7. Make completed output available

              Owner

              GPU completion → native backend → worker

              Interaction

              The backend observes required completion dependencies before consuming results. Prefill/decode passes continue the model's generation work using retained state.

              State change

              The worker can publish output for the corresponding request.

              8. Return output on the response channel

              Owner

              Worker response PUSH → IPC → API response PULL

              Interaction

              The API proxy drains worker responses and associates each response with its request's output stream.

              State change

              The API has a chunk to send; it can still be waiting for later chunks.

              9. Stream bytes using transport flow control

              Owner

              API / Uvicorn → TCP buffers → NIC → client

              Interaction

              The API serializes streamed output. Socket write readiness and transport backpressure determine when more bytes can be sent to a slow reader.

              State change

              The client receives output incrementally while later inference passes may continue.

              10. Finish or cancel request ownership

              Owner

              MAX scheduler and API request lifecycle

              Interaction

              Generation completion releases scheduler membership and request KV ownership. Cancellation travels on its own IPC channel and is handled by the worker; cleanup must respect live device work.

              State change

              Request resources can be reused safely. A retained backing pool and remaining buffered output have separate lifetimes.

              Owner

              Interaction

              4. Submit work with execution dependencies

              Owner

              Native backend / GPU user-space interface

              Interaction

              Device operations are submitted to execution streams and dependencies. Submission can complete on the CPU before the corresponding GPU operation completes.

              State change

              The device has queued work; submitted and finished are different states.

              Owner

              MAX request owner / serving-process owner

              Interaction

              Request cleanup returns cache-page ownership after safe completion. The backing pool and model buffers can remain for the server's lifetime; process/lifespan cleanup releases serving resources on exit.

              Same components, many connections

              A connection, a task and a GPU pass have different lifetimes.

              Thousands of connected clients can share this architecture: Linux holds socket state, the event loop dispatches ready work, and MAX selects inference passes.

              What exists?Who owns it?What it does while waiting
              Connected socketLinux TCP + a process FDCan remain idle or wait while retaining connection state.
              Python taskAPI event loopResumes when network, IPC or executor work is ready.
              Waiting inference requestZeroMQ / MAX schedulerKeeps application state until model work is selected.
              Active inference passWorker + native device backendUses the initialized model and selected request buffers.
              Output waiting to sendAPI / transport / TCP buffersProgress depends on the client and transport readiness.
              many connected sockets
          |
    ready I/O callbacks
          |
   API tasks / local IPC
          |
  queued model requests
          |
 selected inference passes
          |
 output -> API/TCP -> clients

Linux schedules OS threads; uvloop dispatches ready tasks; MAX selects model work.
A connected client does not require its own spawned model-worker process.

              Finite file descriptors, CPU time, host buffers and device capacity still bound the server. A slow reader can hold output buffers after generation has released GPU request ownership.
